units.title: Arguments
units.blurb: What an argument is, how to find its conclusion and premises, and how to lay it out in standard form or as a map.

units.title: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning
units.blurb: Two ways reasons can support a claim: validity and soundness for deduction, strength for induction, and how samples, analogies and causes can mislead.

units.title: Language and Definitions
units.blurb: Clear words make clear arguments: ambiguity and vagueness, kinds of definitions, and how to write and judge a good one.

units.title: Fallacies of Relevance
units.blurb: Arguments whose premises have nothing to do with the conclusion, though they may stir feelings that make them seem to.

units.title: Fallacies of Presumption and Weak Induction
units.blurb: Arguments that sneak in an unearned assumption or leap from too little evidence.

units.title: Fallacies of Ambiguity
units.blurb: Arguments that slide between two meanings of a word, a sentence, or a whole and its parts.

units.title: Evaluating Real Arguments
units.blurb: Putting it all together: conditional fallacies, telling look-alike fallacies apart, reading charitably, and judging an argument step by step.

topics.title: Statements
topics.short: A statement is a sentence that is either true or false; questions, commands and exclamations are not statements.
topics.trouble: Learners think a statement must be true, or that an opinion cannot be a statement. "Pizza is the best food" is a statement; it is just one people disagree about.

topics.title: Arguments and Non-Arguments
topics.short: An argument offers reasons (premises) meant to support a claim (the conclusion); a report, description, warning or bare opinion does not.
topics.trouble: Learners call any passage that states a strong opinion an argument. Without at least one reason offered in support, it is only an assertion.

topics.title: Arguments and Explanations
topics.short: An argument tries to show that something is true; an explanation tells why something we already accept is true.
topics.trouble: The word "because" appears in both. Learners must ask whether the claim is in doubt (argument) or taken as known (explanation).

topics.title: Premises and Conclusions
topics.short: Find the conclusion first by asking what the speaker wants you to believe; the premises are the reasons given for it.
topics.trouble: Learners take the first sentence to be a premise and the last to be the conclusion. The conclusion can come first, last or in the middle.

topics.title: Indicator Words
topics.short: Words like "therefore" and "so" usually mark a conclusion; "because", "since" and "for" usually mark a premise.
topics.trouble: Indicator words have other uses: "since Tuesday" is about time, and "so tired" means very. And many arguments have no indicator words at all.

topics.title: Standard Form
topics.short: Rewrite an argument as numbered premises followed by its conclusion, leaving out filler, repeats and side remarks.
topics.trouble: Learners copy every sentence, including background and asides, or change the meaning of a premise while rewording it.

topics.title: Linked and Convergent Premises
topics.short: Linked premises support the conclusion only together; convergent premises each give a separate reason on their own.
topics.trouble: Learners treat every pair of premises as linked. Test it: if you remove one premise, does the other still give some support by itself?

topics.title: Chains of Reasoning
topics.short: A claim can be the conclusion of one step and a premise of the next; the last claim supported is the main conclusion.
topics.trouble: Learners pick the intermediate conclusion as the main one because it has an indicator word. The main conclusion is the claim everything else finally supports.

topics.title: Unstated Premises
topics.short: Many arguments leave a premise unsaid; supply the most reasonable one that connects the stated premises to the conclusion.
topics.trouble: Learners supply a premise that just repeats the conclusion, or one much stronger than the speaker needs and would accept.

topics.title: Deductive and Inductive Arguments
topics.short: A deductive argument claims its conclusion must be true if the premises are; an inductive argument claims only that it is probably true.
topics.trouble: The old rule "deduction goes from general to specific, induction from specific to general" is not reliable. Ask how strongly the argument claims to support its conclusion.

topics.title: Validity
topics.short: An argument is valid when it is impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false.
topics.trouble: Confusing validity with truth: learners call an argument invalid because a premise is false, or valid because they agree with the conclusion. Validity is about the link, not the facts.

topics.title: Testing Validity with a Counterexample
topics.short: To show a form is invalid, give an argument with the same form whose premises are plainly true and whose conclusion is plainly false.
topics.trouble: Learners change the form while building the counterexample, or pick premises that are not clearly true, so the counterexample proves nothing.

topics.title: Soundness
topics.short: A sound argument is valid and has all true premises, so its conclusion must be true.
topics.trouble: Learners think a true conclusion makes an argument sound. An argument with a true conclusion can still be invalid or have a false premise.

topics.title: Validity and Truth Together
topics.short: Every mix of true and false premises and conclusions is possible for a valid argument except one: true premises with a false conclusion.
topics.trouble: Learners believe a valid argument cannot have false premises or a false conclusion. It can have both; what it cannot have is all true premises and a false conclusion.

topics.title: Strong and Weak Inductive Arguments
topics.short: An inductive argument is strong when its premises, if true, make the conclusion likely; a strong argument with true premises is cogent.
topics.trouble: Learners call strong inductive arguments "valid", or think new evidence cannot change a strong argument. Induction can always be weakened or strengthened by more facts.

topics.title: Generalizing from a Sample
topics.short: A generalization is only as good as its sample: large enough, chosen fairly, and like the whole group in the ways that matter.
topics.trouble: Learners trust a huge sample even when it was chosen in a biased way, such as asking only the people who came to a chess club about favorite games.

topics.title: Arguments from Analogy
topics.short: An analogy argues that two things alike in some ways are alike in another; it is strong when the likenesses are relevant and the differences are not.
topics.trouble: Learners count the number of similarities instead of asking whether they are relevant to the conclusion.

topics.title: Reasoning about Causes
topics.short: Two things happening together does not show that one causes the other; look for a common cause, reverse direction, or coincidence.
topics.trouble: Correlation read as causation: ice cream sales and sunburns rise together because of summer sun, not because one causes the other.

topics.title: Ambiguity and Vagueness
topics.short: A word is ambiguous when it has two distinct meanings in context, and vague when its boundary is fuzzy.
topics.trouble: Learners use the two words as synonyms. "Bat" in "I found a bat" is ambiguous; "tall" is vague, since no exact height separates tall from not tall.

topics.title: Kinds of Definitions
topics.short: Lexical definitions report how a word is used, stipulative ones assign a new meaning, precising ones sharpen a vague word, and persuasive ones slant it.
topics.trouble: Learners judge a stipulative definition as true or false. A new name for a new thing can be clear or unclear, but it cannot be false.

topics.title: Definition by Genus and Difference
topics.short: A classical definition names the larger kind (genus) and the feature that sets this thing apart within it (difference).
topics.trouble: Learners give an example or a synonym instead of a definition, or name a difference that other members of the genus also have.

topics.title: Rules for Good Definitions
topics.short: A good definition is neither too broad nor too narrow, not circular, not negative when it can be positive, and not figurative or obscure.
topics.trouble: Learners mix up too broad and too narrow. Too broad lets in things that do not belong; too narrow shuts out things that do.

topics.title: Emotive and Loaded Language
topics.short: Words can carry feelings as well as facts; loaded words try to win agreement by attitude instead of by reasons.
topics.trouble: Learners think neutral words are always better. Feelings are fine in a speech; the trouble comes when slanted words stand in for evidence.

topics.title: Verbal and Factual Disagreements
topics.short: Some disagreements are about the facts; others vanish once people notice they are using a word in different senses.
topics.trouble: Learners keep arguing about facts when the real disagreement is over what a word means, such as whether a hot dog "counts" as a sandwich.

topics.title: What a Fallacy Is
topics.short: A fallacy is a common pattern of bad reasoning that can look persuasive; formal fallacies are flaws in form, informal ones in content.
topics.trouble: Learners call any false claim a fallacy, or conclude that a fallacious argument has a false conclusion. A bad argument can reach a true conclusion; it just does not show it.

topics.title: Attacking the Person
topics.short: Ad hominem rejects a claim by attacking the person who made it (insults or their circumstances) instead of the reasons given.
topics.trouble: Learners call every criticism of a person ad hominem. Questioning a witness's honesty is fair when the question is whether to trust their report.

topics.title: You Too (Tu Quoque)
topics.short: Tu quoque dismisses an argument because the arguer does not follow their own advice.
topics.trouble: Learners treat hypocrisy as a refutation. A smoker who says smoking harms health may be inconsistent, but the reasons still stand.

topics.title: Straw Man
topics.short: A straw man swaps the opponent's real position for a weaker or exaggerated version, then knocks that down.
topics.trouble: Learners confuse straw man with red herring. A straw man still talks about the opponent's view, only a distorted copy of it.

topics.title: Red Herring
topics.short: A red herring changes the subject to a different issue, then treats the original question as settled.
topics.trouble: Learners call any change of topic a red herring. It is a fallacy when the new topic is used as though it answered the first.

topics.title: Appeal to Force
topics.short: An appeal to force tries to win agreement by a threat of harm instead of by reasons.
topics.trouble: Learners call any warning of a consequence an appeal to force. "If you skip practice, you'll play worse" gives a reason; "agree or you're off the team" gives a threat.

topics.title: Appeal to Pity
topics.short: An appeal to pity asks us to accept a claim because of sympathy, when the sympathy has no bearing on whether the claim is true.
topics.trouble: Feelings are not always irrelevant: hardship can be a good reason for mercy. The fallacy is using pity to show something is true, like that a grade was earned.

topics.title: Appeal to the People
topics.short: The bandwagon fallacy argues that a claim is true, or a choice good, because many people believe it or do it.
topics.trouble: Learners call any mention of popularity a fallacy. Popularity is relevant to claims about popularity itself ("this is the best-selling book").

topics.title: Appeals to Authority: Fair and Unfair
topics.short: Citing an expert in their own field, where experts agree, is reasonable; citing someone outside their expertise, or one voice against a consensus, is not.
topics.trouble: Learners think every appeal to authority is a fallacy. We rely on experts all the time; the questions are whether this is their field and whether they are trustworthy here.

topics.title: Appeal to Ignorance
topics.short: An appeal to ignorance argues that a claim is true because it has not been shown false, or false because it has not been shown true.
topics.trouble: A careful search that finds nothing can be evidence ("we checked every room; the cat is not inside"). The fallacy treats a mere lack of proof as proof.

topics.title: Begging the Question
topics.short: An argument begs the question when a premise assumes the very conclusion it is supposed to prove, often in other words.
topics.trouble: In everyday speech "begs the question" means "raises the question". In logic it means circular reasoning: the conclusion hides in a premise.

topics.title: Complex Question
topics.short: A complex question has a hidden assumption built in, so that any direct answer grants it.
topics.trouble: Learners answer the question instead of spotting the assumption. "Have you stopped forgetting your homework?" assumes you used to forget it.

topics.title: False Dilemma
topics.short: A false dilemma presents two options as the only ones when others exist.
topics.trouble: Learners treat every either-or as a false dilemma. "The light is on or it is off" really does cover the cases; the fallacy needs a missing option.

topics.title: Hasty Generalization
topics.short: A hasty generalization draws a conclusion about a whole group from a sample that is too small or not typical.
topics.trouble: Learners confuse it with accident. Hasty generalization goes from a few cases up to a rule; accident applies a good rule down to a case it does not fit.

topics.title: False Cause
topics.short: False cause claims one thing caused another only because it came first (post hoc) or because the two occur together.
topics.trouble: Learners accept "it happened right after, so it caused it". Timing is a clue, not a proof; look for other causes and for chance.

topics.title: Slippery Slope
topics.short: A slippery slope claims one step will set off a chain of bad results, without good reason to think each link will happen.
topics.trouble: Some chains are well supported. The fallacy is a chain of weak or unsupported links presented as though the end were certain.

topics.title: Weak Analogy
topics.short: A weak analogy rests on likenesses that do not matter for the conclusion, or ignores differences that do.
topics.trouble: Learners call every comparison weak. Ask what the conclusion needs, then check whether the two cases share that feature.

topics.title: Suppressed Evidence
topics.short: Suppressed evidence leaves out an important fact that would change the conclusion.
topics.trouble: Learners check only whether the stated premises are true. A set of true premises can still mislead when a key fact is left out.

topics.title: Accident
topics.short: Accident applies a general rule to a special case that the rule was never meant to cover.
topics.trouble: Learners call this hasty generalization. Here the rule is fine in general; the mistake is forcing it onto an exception, like ticketing an ambulance for speeding.

topics.title: Equivocation
topics.short: Equivocation uses a word in one sense in one premise and in another sense elsewhere, so the argument only seems to connect.
topics.trouble: The shift in meaning is easy to miss because the spelling stays the same. Replace the word with its meaning in each line and the gap shows.

topics.title: Amphiboly
topics.short: Amphiboly draws a conclusion from a sentence whose grammar allows two readings.
topics.trouble: Learners confuse amphiboly with equivocation. In equivocation one word has two meanings; in amphiboly the sentence structure does.

topics.title: Composition
topics.short: Composition reasons that because every part has a property, the whole must have it too.
topics.trouble: Some properties do carry over (if every brick is red, the wall is red). Learners must ask whether this property is one that adds up.

topics.title: Division
topics.short: Division reasons that because the whole has a property, each part must have it too.
topics.trouble: Learners mix up composition and division. Composition goes from parts to the whole; division goes from the whole to the parts.

topics.title: Affirming the Consequent and Denying the Antecedent
topics.short: From "if P then Q", you may infer Q from P, and not-P from not-Q; inferring P from Q, or not-Q from not-P, is a fallacy.
topics.trouble: Affirming the consequent feels natural: "If it rained, the street is wet. The street is wet, so it rained." A sprinkler could have wet the street.

topics.title: Telling Look-Alike Fallacies Apart
topics.short: Name the fallacy by the job the faulty step does: distorting a view, changing the subject, leaping from a sample, or assuming the conclusion.
topics.trouble: Learners match on surface words ("everyone", "expert") rather than on what the reasoning does. Find the faulty step first, then name it.

topics.title: Good Reasoning That Looks Like a Fallacy
topics.short: Many fallacy names have fair cousins: trusted experts, well-supported chains of causes, and real either-or choices are good reasoning.
topics.trouble: Fallacy hunting: learners shout a fallacy name at every argument they dislike. Each name fits only when its faulty step is really there.

topics.title: The Principle of Charity
topics.short: Before judging an argument, state it in its strongest reasonable form, the way its author would accept.
topics.trouble: Learners read charity as agreeing. Charity is about understanding the argument fairly; you may still find it weak after that.

topics.title: Evaluating an Argument Step by Step
topics.short: Find the conclusion and premises, check whether the reasoning is valid or strong, then check whether the premises are true.
topics.trouble: Learners jump to "I disagree with the conclusion" without asking the two separate questions: does it follow, and are the premises true?

topics.title: Objections and Replies
topics.short: A strong case answers the best objection to it; an objection attacks a premise or the link from premises to conclusion.
topics.trouble: Learners answer a weak objection, or think an objection to one premise defeats a conclusion that has other, independent support.
